Descrições de atuações frias, mecânicas e falta de química entre os atores; a recitação dos diálogos é vista como artificial e desconectada da realidade emocional necessária.
Incapacidade do filme em criar suspense ou atmosfera inquietante; as cenas que deveriam assustar apenas geram tédio e frustração, deixando o público indiferente.

amostra_completa.texto: DULL. Horror movie it definitely isn’t. There is nothing remotely scary or hair rising or even creepy about it. Unless a carved x on a chest is what defines this as horror. Critique on Japanese society. Perhaps. But without any other context (which there isn’t) it just feels like a bad arty song lyric sheet. Clinical and elliptical approach that slowly lures you into the narrative. Clinical it is indeed. Did it lure me in? Definitely not. On the contrary this sterile approach has nothing else on it to lure, so it just became more distant from me minute after minute. I was watching with the same apathy that the people were performing murders. To be frank this movie was so horribly bad that I felt what the guy in the opening scene bashing the head of the prostitute with a water pipe felt: absolutely nothing.

Maybe things were different in 1997 but the true horror was the agonizingly slow pace of this movie. No amount of "no, the real question is who are you?" makes this psychological or introspective more than it makes it annoying. After a few minutes of typical detective film we're left to suffer a series of frames moved along by a series of scenes and nothing of note. There's blood and there's bodies, because of course there have to be, but names, faces, and places that are so easily forgotten that they might as well not have been anything. If content is the thing in the box, then this film is all wrapping paper and nothing of substance. Atmosphere for atmosphere sake. It's up to the detectives to figure out the "complex mind of a criminal" but this dude doesn't even know why he's doing it either. At some point he gets hypnotized by what amounts to ye olde books on tape and some liberal arts classes then prances from place to place playing at the arrogant ass with amnesia. The real "villain" is an unknown catalyst from 200 years ago and a few handwaving woo woo concepts like power of suggestion and alchemy for no reason. Main detective's sick wife was an initial thread of intrigue, that turned into nothing, and then she was tucked away until the very heavily telegraphed shock value scene. But at least main detective emptied his clip into that guy before very expectedly becoming that guy.

everything about this movie from its theme and subtext to its pacing, dialogue, and atmosphere is unbearably dull. the characters bored me, and maybe if at least one of them had been remotely intriguing i would have found something to hold onto, but there was nothing special about any of them. i genuinely have no idea what people see in this. it’s rated ridiculously high and the level of glazing is insane, maybe they’ve lost their minds too.

DNF 47:40 Every scene is this slow, methodical and static long-take and i’m sorry i just can’t take it. My mind can’t handle films with less than 5 cuts a second. I get so, so, so bored. I also think i just don’t like Japanese storytelling. Miyazaki, Kurosawa, most of Miike and Oshii’s work i’ve more or less bounced off. I’ve found the large majority of the anime i’ve seen to be dull. Even the stuff i’ve liked has generally been less for the storytelling and more because they are filled with action or a certain big lizard. Smarter people than i have told me that the Japanese generally has a completely different approach to storytelling and structure than most countries and maybe that’s why it doesn’t connect with me. Or maybe i’m just horribly racist. Who knows?

tenia muchisimas ganas de ver esta pelicula y me he llevado una decepcion tremenda. que horror. para empezar es una pelicula con una ausencia increible de tension narrativa y no, no tiene nada que ver con que el ritmo sea pausado, para mi eso no es un problema. el problema es que aunque el ritmo sea pausado no estas avanzando, las escenas no tienen un proposito narrativo claro. es siempre lo mismo, una repeticion sin crecimiento ni consecuencias. no hay progresion dramatica, no hay giros, no hay revelaciones. solo una sucesion de escenas que se parecen demasiado entre si, sin tension interna ni verdadero conflicto. por ejemplo en se7en los asesinatos iban revelando pequeñas cosas y se iba completando todo como un puzzle con todos esos avances, pero aqui no hay una progresion, simplemente se repite lo mismo durante practicamente 1h. la historia y el guion son realmente flojos. la trama es repetitiva y no ofrece nada nuevo ni sorprendente; se limita a mostrar una y otra vez el mismo patron sin profundizar en sus causas ni en las consecuencias de los hechos. los dialogos son escasos y muchas veces vacios, sin aportar desarrollo a los personajes ni al conflicto central. la repeticion excesiva desgasta la tension en lugar de construirla. ademas los personajes son excesivamente planos, no aportan nada. no me han movido por dentro ni para bien ni para mal, me han dejado indiferente. una historia que no tiene nada interesante que contar, no se desarrolla, y podria contarse en 10 minutos. no hay complejidad, ni tan siquiera una direccion brillante, nada. es literalmente anodina , que es lo peor que puedes hacer: una pelicula que no tiene nada especial ni para bien ni para mal. no genera ni miedo ni suspense ni asco ni nada. no se genera una atmosfera de interes, nada de nada. yo soy una persona que se fija muchisimo en los personajes, me tienen que atraer, por su frialdad, por su magnetismo, por su violencia, por su lo que sea. tambien me fijo en una buena historia, si tiene escenas largas y lentas que su guion sea brillante por lo menos, que se genere una tension enorme o se utilicen grandes planos. tiene que haber al menos algo por dios y aqui nada. decepcionante.

I signed up for the Criterion Channel just to watch this. Cure was a massive disappointment. One of those films that makes me go crazy...questioning why it is held in such high regard. I can take slow burn, abstract and subliminal. What I can’t take is obtuse, uninteresting, pretentious and worst of all boring. Cure seems to be aiming for the former but feels more like the latter. This is a slog of a movie, without a single character to latch unto or care about and a mystery that is not as interesting as it pretends to be, even after lifting the veil of symbolism behind it. The idea of a hypnotist serial killer that brings out the violent suppressed desires of a repressed and tired society of seemingly innocent human beings is all well and good, but the storytelling here by director Kiyoshi Kurosawa just did not work for me at all. Cure is a mind bender of a movie I have no desire to analyze as I found nothing about it to be worthy of my time. It’s been a while since I actively disliked a movie that I know has artistry, thought and effort behind it, yet I could not connect with any of it.

I could have watched 2 Hisayasu Satô movies instead of this. So of course, I chose wrong. I really wanted to like this film. With the reviews, I expected an immediate masterpiece that could hypnotize me. But there's nothing here. It's limp. Too clean. Sterile. Safe. There's no moods here. No longing. Alienation. Nihilism. Nothing beautiful to look at. Nothing grotesque. Nothing grungy. The edges have been sanded off and talked away. Even if he survives on the worst VHS transfers, Satô is the 90s. He paints in beautiful blues, captures the coldness of the city, and its strangeness. "Cure" is never shocking nor even eerie or dream-like. It's a dull procedural far too conventional in plot and cinematography for me. This is somewhat the same struggle I had with " Trouble Every Day " (2001) recently, but that film was worse and suffered from terrible acting from the husband (Vincent Gallo) and his wife. No one is a bad actor in "Cure," but I want someone to possess me here. My husband asked me if we're jaded. I disagree: I'm worshipping and throwing five stars at the alter of Jess Franco (and I can't convince him to share that delusion). I can handle slow, aimless plots that are pure cinematic dreams. I can handle Criterion films with slower pacing: like my 5 stars for both "Belle de Jour" and "The Night Porter." Hypnosis just doesn't work on all people.

I didn’t enjoy it. Maybe it’s the fact it’s a thriller, maybe it’s the fact that it was rather austere, but this Japanese film of the 90s didn’t draw me in at all. It just felt sort of dragging and not particularly engaging. And reading other people’s critiques and takes does show that this film captivates others in a way that it could not with me. Sometimes it just doesn’t click, it’s not the film’s fault. It might be my state of mind that just needed something lighter. This is essentially social critque expressed through the lens of the horror genre. The story follows a detective investigating a string of murders where an X is carved into the neck of each victim, the murderer is found near the victim of each case and remembers nothing of the crime. The detective is a repressed, cold man who looks after his unstable wife. The film is driven by his desire to understand the workings of the man who can seemingly hypnotise people, getting them to commit heinous crimes. While trying to figure all of this out, his own mind starts to slip, losing sense of what is real and what not. If you like tense, austere horror / thriller — this will be perfect. I, turns out, am not particularly excited by it.

An inept detective tracks down a serial killer who hypnotizes people by mimicking the annoying questions of a seven year old. I am baffled by the love for this movie. The acting is laughably bad, the dialogue is barely functional, the plot is nearly non-existent. My best guess as to why people like this film is its insufferable dedication to being “mysterious”. The only mystery here is how someone could cobble together such a half-assed production. If as other reviewers suggest, the film is riffing on the idea that there is violence within all of us that we suppress out of some loyalty to social norms, then this is a movie I want to watch, not some convoluted nonsense about a century-old hypnotist whose dark art of drawing Xs in the air resurfaces in 90s in the form of a serial killer. This is a movie that is half-committed to a great idea but abandons its other half to schlocky genius-psychopath tropes and hammy psychobabble. And seriously, not one actor changed their clothes the whole movie. There are two things worth remembering about this otherwise boring film, the sound design which blends mechanical ambient noise with a a sound mix that puts incidental noises and the voices front and center, and the effectively creepy art direction that feels almost post-apocalyptic at times and in a better movie would have been utilized to tell us something about the world and the characters we see on screen. I’m going to give Kurosawa one more chance with Pulse but after Spy’s Wife and Cure I can’t see my opinion changing much.

Spooktober 2024: Day 25 watching a horror movie Truly sorry, folks, but I seriously don’t get the hype for this. Throughout it's protracted runtime, i found Cure excruciatingly overstays it's welcome, by spinning out in a mystery that leads nowhere significant. To be fair, the premise itself is thoroughly intriguing: a killer feigning amnesia, endowed with a disquieting aura and a hypnotic prowess that allows him to tap into the subconscious of others, compelling them to commit heinous acts of violence without their cognizance. Such concept is actually rife with potential for exploration into the sinister recesses of human psychology. Yet, alas, the execution is agonizingly elongated, dragging it's feet through a mire of monotony that offers neither excitement nor genuine intrigue. Instead of gripping suspense or tension, we’re given repetitive interrogations and a mystery that barely unfolds, with Detective Takabe going in circles without ever yielding anything fruitful. There's also hardly any dramatic tension from Takabe’s personal family life, which could have added much-needed stakes, yet it's barely developed. As for Cure being labeled as “horror” is just wildly exaggerated & preposterous. There is scarcely any signs of the ominous, the horrific, let alone the thrills to be found within it's frames. Sure, it leans into police procedural thriller territory, but unlike other renowned crime films that takes advantage of dark atmospheres, intense thrills and menacing villain, yet Cure chooses instead to meander, devoid of the tension that one might reasonably expect. As for the ending, it is just okay at best, or perhaps an anticlimactic denouement to an otherwise excruciatingly drawn-out narrative. Overall, for lack of a better word, Cure is basically just nothing burger, and a snoozefest, wrapped up in an overrated hype that it doesn’t live up to. In the end, I confess I am at a loss to understand it's appeal, and I find myself utterly indifferent to the exalted status it has amassed within cinematic discourse. Perhaps some among you might wish to send me to the guillotine for this audacious opinion, so i’ll evade for a bit!🤐 However, i'll definitely be back soon after my rewatch for a review from a movie what i consider a truly profound horror experience, that is The Substance (2024), to cleanse my palate and to appropriately conclude this Halloween season. Day 11 of 31 🎃 The movie starts with a series of strange murders: ordinary people killing others, and all the victims have an “X” marked on their bodies. The creepy part is that the killers don’t know why they did it, which creates a mystery from the very beginning. Mamiya, the strange student who connects all the crimes, is super stressful. At one point, he even made me laugh, because he kept repeating the same things over and over without really saying anything. I felt just like Detective Takabe, lost and trying to make sense of it all. However, I found the movie very slow and boring. I understand that for some people, the slow pace and psychological horror might be interesting, but for me, it was hard to enjoy. The tension and mystery they try to create didn’t really grab me. That’s why my rating is 2 out of 5 stars. Maybe someone else will enjoy it, but for me, it was just too slow and not exciting enough🎃

It's hard not to appreciate the amazing acting going on in CURE, in particular, the performance of Koji Yakusho but despite some gut-wrenching emotion and power punches of anger, the displays of acting ability are overshadowed by a very bland & uninteresting story that is (intentionally?) obvious from kill #2 before blandly teasing higher powers at work. I can't say I didn't enjoy looking at the movie, the use of locations, inside and outside, gave an interesting look at Tokyo and surrounding areas. When the film focuses on the gruesome, it does hit a home run and while using it sparingly, it does so effectively. A huge influence to J-horror of the coming years for sure, I would have just preferred a straight-up serial killer chase as opposed to anything more.

Probably no one should go into a movie they've heard is "the greatest movie ever," perhaps except "The Godfather," which can still withstand the onslaught of the highest expectations. In this case, director Ari Aster has said "Cure" possibly is such. Watching this and knowing his filmography, you can see all of the connections.  Also, the ones with Bong Joon-ho. In truth I would rather rewatch Aster or Joon-ho, even though I do like Kurosawa. One strong element coming up here is the subject matter.  In this time period you get plenty of films with serial killers, some often feeling that a rationalization for their killings or methods is necessary.  What's tackled in "Cure," and this is possibly a mild spoiler, is hypnotism. If you know the topic decently well, you can see when a script is handwaving.  Here it's the scene where the detective inquires about whether a subject can be hypnotized into killing someone.  The answer is "no," you can't, because it's darn near impossible for a practicing hynoptist to make you do something against your will and to violate your self-sure identity.  In other words, if you aren't a killer and don't want to, a master hypnotist can't just come up to you, "make you sleepy," and then get you to off a rando. This movies presumes that to be the case, so it goes beyond believability to me.  I am one who often calls movies "hypnotic experiences," because they are.  They induce trance-like states in suggestible people. Guilty as charged. To go about hypnotism for a minute, the subject is fascinating when it's consider at a more mundane level, where it is in fact often wielded insidiously.  Take any marketing class for proof.  Just yesterday, picking up a prescription, the pharmacist nearly got me to bite on a couple of inoculations.  She was decent-looking, she used quite persuasive language on the level of good marketers and hypnotists, and I was already suggestible towards "eradicating' bad diseases.  What I had to do was pause and say to myself, "decide later," which I did. This is not easy for almost all of us.  Some philosophers and hypnotists have suggested that because we all always somewhat suggestible, we may not have "free will."  I have no opinion on that matter, though the unconscious mind does control an awful lot, does it not? Anyway, "Cure" is effectively a slowburn detective thriller that uses this topic as its basis for proceeding.  It may be credibly watched as a discussion on the topic as well, which is where I object to what it's portraying. As a slowburn, ala Aster movies, it occasionally shocks successfully. A director like Aster could learn much from the setups and payoffs here, especially the takes that don't cut and then shock. That wouldn't make this the greatest movie ever, not even a good movie; just an effective one at using certain techniques at certain times. Unfairly, perhaps, I'm reminded of David Fincher's work -- "Se7en" did come out before this -- "Memories of Murder," S. Craig Zahler's work, ad infinitum. A bunch of those I'd rather rewatch rather than this one, to state a personal preference.  To put all cards on the table, I've always loved the stuff that has flair a bit more than those that don't: Welles, Gilliam, etc. There's surely more to this movie than anybody can examine, a truism of mediocre to bad movies too! But there's so little time, and so much to watch. I'd rather have somebody else and some other movie hypnotize me.

English Version below Nachdem Longlegs ein als Thriller verkleideter Horrorfilm war, dachte ich mir, dass es an der Zeit wäre, weitere Filme dieser seltenen Kategorie zu sichten. Zufällig gab mir ein guter Freund den Impuls, es mit Cure zu versuchen. Der 90er Jahre Japan-Horror erfreut sich global großer Beleibtheit und war mir in den letzten Jahren häufiger in diversen Listen oder Kritiken begegnet. Und recht schnell stelle ich hier sehr deutliche Parallelen zu Longlegs fest, denn die Ausgangslage der Hauptfigur ist hier nahezu identisch. Doch Cure leidet inhaltlich stark darunter, dass sich der Film unglaublich ernst nimmt und leider genau dies nicht ist. Die Figuren handeln zu oft derart unplausibel, dass es mich mehrfach aus der Geschichte rausgehauen hat, weil ich es nicht ertragen konnte, wie unglaubwürdig dumm hier agiert wurde. Ärgerlich ist hierbei besonders, dass dadurch jegliche Spannung verloren ging, da man auch den Antagonisten nicht mehr ernst nehmen konnte. Dabei sind Szenenbild und Sound durchaus gelungen. Und die Prämisse, in einem Lichtstrahl, einem Feuerschein, einem Windhauch oder nur im Umblättern von Notizbüchern eine Gefahr zu wähnen, ist durchaus ambitioniert und gelingt sogar einige Male. Denn dass man nur einen Feuerzeugschein vom totalen Kontrollverlust entfernt ist, bringt der Film in vielen Stellen deutlich auf den Punkt. Die Idee und die Inszenierung sind zum Großteil gut. Leider sorgen die Schwächen der Geschichte und die hölzerne Darstellung dafür, dass die Gefahr nur selten bei mir ankam. Das Ende ist dann inhaltlich ebenfalls nicht mehr meins, da der Film für diese nihilistische Note dann gar nicht düster genug war. Die überschwänglichen Bewertungen kann ich mir nur so erklären, dass hier Mesmerismus am Werk war. ------------------------------- After *Longlegs* turned out to be a horror film disguised as a thriller, I thought it was time to explore more movies in this rare category. Coincidentally, a good friend suggested that I try *Cure*. 90s Japanese horror enjoys great global popularity and has appeared frequently in various lists or reviews in recent years. I quickly noticed very clear parallels to *Longlegs*, as the main character's initial situation is almost identical. However, *Cure* suffers greatly from the fact that the film takes itself incredibly seriously, but unfortunately, it doesn't quite succeed in that regard. The characters act so implausibly that it pulled me out of the story multiple times because I couldn’t bear how unbelievably foolish their actions were. What’s particularly frustrating is that this completely eroded any tension, as it also made it impossible to take the antagonist seriously. That said, the set design and sound are quite well done. And the premise of perceiving danger in a beam of light, a flicker of flame, a gust of wind, or even just in the turning of notebook pages is certainly ambitious and succeeds a few times. The film effectively conveys that one is just a flicker of a lighter away from total loss of control at many points. The idea and the execution are mostly good. Unfortunately, the weaknesses in the story and the wooden performances meant that the sense of danger rarely reached me. The ending also didn’t sit well with me, as the film wasn’t dark enough to justify this nihilistic note. I can only explain the rave reviews by assuming that mesmerism was at work here.

Kiyoshi Kurosawa's Hypnotism Doesn't Work on Me Listen, I'm not trying to be an angry contrarian but...holy cinepheliac fucking fuck does Letterboxd glaze the cinematic shit out of this movie (and director, actually). Not me. I like hearing all opinions. I've read enough. I've seen...enough. I had to doom-scroll to find any critical reviews and even then, they are mostly drowning in film nerd pretension (thank you to people who don't feel the need to close read film themes). Shoutout to all the meme reviews. My search tells me people either actually love this film or have been fooled--perhaps even bullied--into loving it. Not me. I was so fucking bored. Let's talk about why. Respect to any and all who found any joy watching this (sorry that hypnotism works on you). This review is not for you. This is my third Kurosawa film. I know his style. He's here for the big mood. He wants us hypnotized. And he is definitely a competent filmmaker. He loves his ambient noise. He loves bridge shots. He loves a panning camera. He loves natural light. And as a mood piece, this style works. If that's all every movie ever (ever) was...I'd literally burn down the world and laugh until my head came off. I watch movies to have fun and escape my shitty little life. Not to be numb. Cure is cinematic anesthesia. As compelling as the narrative is in spades, it's not remotely exciting paired with the delirious ennui of the film's introspective direction where I just feel a whole lot of nothing the whole time. Or, in simpler words, the mood behind the direction gets in the way of the film's plot for me and makes me feel empty. Maybe that's the point but it doesn't mean I have to agree. I think it's pretentious bullshit. Give me resolution or give me death. Make me feel something or go fuck yourself. I've read people speak on the realism of this film. Unfortunately, these aren't real people (you are not real people) and they don't feel real either (you don't feel real). We have an angry detective, his crazy wife, and a defiant third character. It's not compelling. I am not compelled. It's impersonal. It's apathetic. It's cold and the cold feels calculated. It might even be misanthropic. It is objectively a nihilist film. And worst of all? I actually almost like it. It's a painful type of indifference I rarely encounter in media and for that, I say, fuck it: I'll keep watching Kurosawa movies until one makes me feel something. (*^▽^)/★*☆♪ Neither recommended nor...not recommended (yes I am crying about it),  2.5/5.

Very moody in a post-Se7en way, this horror-themed crime drama sadly doesn't live up to its early promise. Kôji Yakusho puts in a strong performance as Takabe, a murder detective whose latest case threatens to break his brain. An epidemic seems to be emerging in Tokyo, in which ordinary people suddenly snap and brutally kill a loved one or colleague, each time in the same specific way that has a strange, ritualistic element. When questioned by Takabe, none of these killers can explain why they did it, and are also afflicted by amnesia, which connects them to a strange young man with the memory of a goldfish. So far, so intriguing - and there's at least one splash of seriously gruesome gore - but as Takabe starts to piece together a rational explanation for all this (by horror movie standards, that is), the mystery that's made it so interesting all but vanishes, just leaving unbelievable pseudo-science. There is a cracker of a shock moment at one point, involving Takabe's mentally ill wife, but unfortunately the film doesn't pursue that particular line of plot development in any meaningful way.

As horrific and unnerving as this was, I think there’s something missing Kiyoshi Kurosawa has an amazing ability when it comes to ambiguity. He can create mysteries like no other, but I don’t know why I couldn’t connect with this story. I love how it delves into the supernatural stuff, hypnotism- it’s all interesting. I just feel like there should’ve been more than just ambiguity . I was bored most of the time. I thought the story would pick up after the opening, but it just got boring, to entertaining, to boring again, and so on. It wasn’t fun. I’d rather watch Zodiac again, and I’ve seen that film five times already! I can’t connect with Kurosawa. I’ve seen Creepy (2016) & To The Ends of The Earth (2021) and I felt empty. Completely empty. Are there any other Kurosawa films that I should try before I avoid his films altogether
